entries.name: graphify
entries.summary: Turns a repository into a queryable code/knowledge graph.
entries.why: Foundry's context provider uses the graphify CLI to hand workers only the relevant files and symbols instead of whole files — the single biggest token saver during Clarify and each Attempt.

source.install: uv tool install graphifyy && graphify install --platform claude

codex.install: uv tool install graphifyy && graphify install --platform codex

entries.name: tdd
entries.summary: Red → green → refactor discipline with deep-module guidance.
entries.why: Workers that write the failing test first produce changes the engine's command checks can verify, and far fewer 'fix the test instead of the bug' attempts.

workflow.instruction: Before writing implementation code, invoke it and follow red → green → refactor through public interfaces; keep the failing test in the diff and run single test files often, the full suite once at the end.
Invoke it first: pin the current behaviour with tests through public interfaces, then restructure in small green steps.

entries.name: diagnosing-bugs
entries.summary: Systematic root-cause diagnosis instead of guess-and-patch.
entries.why: Retry attempts receive a failure report; this skill makes the worker reproduce and localise before editing, which is what turns attempt #2 into a pass.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it before editing: reproduce → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → add a regression test. Report the reproduction you built.

entries.name: code-review
entries.summary: Structured review checklist focused on correctness and design.
entries.why: Gives the task and goal reviewers a consistent rubric, so blockers are real blockers and style nits stay out.

workflow.instruction: Use its two axes (Standards and Spec) on the whole diff; the base branch named under "Fixed point" is your fixed point.

entries.name: ponytail
entries.summary: Lazy senior dev mode: the smallest change that fully solves the task, reusing what the codebase, the standard library and the installed dependencies already have.
entries.why: Workers stop at the first rung that holds — does it need to exist, is it already here, does the platform do it — so goals ship less code with the same validation, error handling and tests. Per goal: the Ponytail switch.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it first and climb its ladder before you write: nothing new when the codebase, the standard library, the platform or an installed dependency already does it; the smallest complete change, callers, tests and fixtures included; never cut validation, error handling, security or accessibility. When a TDD rule applies here too, TDD decides how tests are written and Ponytail how much code. End your result with what you skipped or did not check and any risk.

Invoke it first: grep every caller of what you touch, fix the root cause once in the shared code, and change nothing the fix does not need. When the diagnosing-bugs rule applies too, follow its steps; Ponytail decides how much code. End your result with what you skipped or did not check and any risk.
Read it before carving tasks: plan only what the goal needs, reuse what the repository already has, and never plan a task for flexibility nobody asked for.

entries.name: ponytail-review
entries.summary: Reviews a change like the senior dev who gets paged: the code it touches, not only the diff — bugs, security, real load, missing tests, speed, what to cut.
entries.why: Each finding names a concrete case, the fix and what happens if it is skipped, so blockers are real and the rest stays advice. Replaces code-review while the goal's Ponytail switch is on.

workflow.instruction: Review with it: read the code the change touches, not only the diff. Only its Must fix findings (a bug, a security hole, data loss, breaking at the expected load) are blockers; put its Should fix and Nice to have findings in your notes, each with its concrete case.

entries.name: ponytail-audit
entries.summary: Maps the whole repository and ranks what to fix first: bugs, security, load, missing tests, speed, code to cut.
entries.why: The optional audit at the end of a goal runs it on the finished branch: Must fix findings in the code the goal touched become fix tasks before the final review, the rest is listed for a follow-up.

entries.name: grilling
entries.summary: Relentless clarifying interview technique for plans.
entries.why: The Clarifier gets one shot at the Brief; this skill sharpens how it turns ambiguity into explicit assumptions and the few questions that are truly blocking.

entries.name: domain-modeling
entries.summary: Name the concepts precisely before designing code.
entries.why: Better task specs: the Planner splits work along real domain boundaries instead of file counts, which is what makes parallel tasks merge cleanly.

workflow.instruction: Read it for vocabulary discipline only — you are read-only: do not write CONTEXT.md or ADRs.

entries.name: codebase-design
entries.summary: Deep modules, simple interfaces, code an AI can navigate.
entries.why: Keeps workers from scattering a feature across many shallow files — fewer files touched means fewer merge conflicts and cheaper reviews.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it when you introduce or reshape a module: prefer deep modules with small interfaces.
Use its deep-module vocabulary when carving tasks.

entries.name: webapp-testing
entries.summary: Portable Playwright guidance from Anthropic; requires Python, Python Playwright and Chromium.
entries.why: Lets a worker actually exercise a UI change end-to-end instead of declaring victory after unit tests.

entries.name: frontend-design
entries.summary: Anthropic's guidance for producing distinctive, production-grade frontends.
entries.why: Useful when goals include UI work; not needed for backend-only repositories. Portable design instructions; compatible with Claude Code and Codex without an Anthropic account.

workflow.instruction: Read it before writing any markup or styles; choose a deliberate aesthetic direction for this product and apply it consistently instead of templated defaults.

entries.name: ui-ux-pro-max
entries.summary: Searchable design databases: styles, palettes, font pairings, product types, UX guidelines, icons, motion presets.
entries.why: Gives UI work a concrete, researched direction (style, palette, typography) before the first line of CSS.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it first with the product type and audience to get a style, palette, font pairing and UX guidelines; build the UI on that recommendation and say which one you followed.
Check the delivered UI against its UX guidelines (hierarchy, spacing, contrast, states) and name concrete violations.

entries.name: impeccable
entries.summary: /impeccable: craft, polish, critique, audit and 19 more sub-commands for intentional, non-generic frontends.
entries.why: One command family for building UI and for reviewing it; its critique doubles as a design review. Uses the selected backend’s native skill. Foundry sessions do not enable Codex child agents; use the skill’s documented serial fallback when delegation is unavailable.

workflow.instruction: Run `/impeccable craft` for new UI or `/impeccable polish` for existing UI before you consider the task done; never ship the generic defaults it warns about.
Run `/impeccable critique` on the delivered UI and turn its findings into concrete pass/fail notes.

entries.name: bencium-impact-designer
entries.summary: Bencium's impact designer: distinctive production UI that avoids the generic AI aesthetic.
entries.why: Opinionated direction for UI tasks, built on Anthropic's frontend-design guidance.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it before building UI and follow its direction for layout, colour and type; avoid the patterns it lists as generic.

entries.name: design-audit
entries.summary: Systematic visual audit that ends in a phased implementation plan.
entries.why: Gives the goal reviewer a structured way to judge UI quality.

workflow.instruction: Audit the delivered UI with it and report only concrete defects that a fix task could act on.

entries.name: typography
entries.summary: Typography rules: quotes, dashes, spacing, hierarchy.
entries.why: Small, mechanical wins on every text-heavy UI.

workflow.instruction: Apply its rules to headings and body copy you write or touch.

entries.name: web-design-engineer
entries.summary: ConardLi's web-design-engineer: pages, landing pages, dashboards and prototypes from 25 design recipes.
entries.why: Recipe-driven UI construction with a strong visual baseline.

workflow.instruction: Pick the recipe that matches the page type before building, and follow it for structure, spacing and colour.

entries.name: web-video-presentation
entries.summary: Turns scripts or articles into click-driven 16:9 web presentations (23 themes).
entries.why: For goals whose output is a presentation rather than an app.

workflow.instruction: Build the deliverable with this skill: script → outline → click-driven 16:9 web presentation (optional narration audio). List every produced page/asset in the task manifest.
When the task asks for a presentation or slide deck as a web page, build it with this skill.

entries.name: autoskills
entries.summary: Detects the repository stack and installs matching project skills (.claude/skills for Claude; .agents/skills for Codex).
entries.why: Workers get framework-specific house rules for the exact stack they are editing; Foundry runs it per goal in the goal workspace.

source.install: npx -y autoskills@latest --dry-run   # needs Node >= 22; Foundry runs it for you in each goal workspace

entries.name: claude-api
entries.summary: Optional reference for projects using the Anthropic API / SDK; usable by either engine.
entries.why: Use only when the project itself integrates Anthropic services. This is SDK reference material, not a Claude runtime requirement or a Foundry login mode. Project API credentials are separate from Foundry’s ChatGPT subscription login.

entries.name: skill-creator
entries.summary: Anthropic's skill for writing new skills well.
entries.why: For people who want to add their own entries to this catalog. Its evaluation and description-optimization flows depend on Claude CLI; Codex uses the separate OpenAI skill-creator entry.

entries.name: skill-creator
entries.summary: OpenAI’s Codex-native guide for creating and maintaining skills.
entries.why: For adding skills to Codex without requiring Claude CLI or Claude-specific evaluation tooling. If an older Anthropic copy is already installed, use Replace to select this version; the old copy goes to trash.

entries.name: gstack
entries.summary: Garry Tan's large skill suite (review, QA, ship, design…).
entries.why: Powerful but heavyweight: it is a git clone that flattens ~60 skills into ~/.claude/skills and installs its own hooks, so it must be installed and upgraded with its own tooling, not copied by Foundry. This catalog recipe is for Claude only. Upstream’s experimental Codex port uses separate setup and requires authenticated Claude CLI for outside reviews; it is not part of Foundry’s ChatGPT-only setup.

entries.name: prototype
entries.summary: Throwaway code that answers one question: a terminal app for logic, or several radically different UI variants.
entries.why: Research tasks should produce knowledge, not production code; the prototype discipline keeps spikes cheap and disposable.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it: build the smallest throwaway that answers the question, write the answer down, and do not polish.

entries.name: research
entries.summary: Primary-source research that ends in cited Markdown.
entries.why: When a goal points at external docs or links, a disciplined research pass beats guessing.

workflow.instruction: When the goal or its attachments point at external documentation, invoke it to ground the Brief in primary sources.

entries.name: gpt-image-2
entries.summary: Image generation/editing skill for GPT Image 2: 80+ structured prompt templates (posters, UI, product shots, infographics, comics), generates via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint or hands the engineered prompt to the host agent.
entries.why: The image pack: image tasks need a disciplined prompt + generation flow instead of ad-hoc API calls. ChatGPT sign-in does not supply image API credentials or desktop-only image tools; without a configured image backend, use its prompt-only mode.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it first: pick the matching template, engineer the prompt, then generate. Independent images MUST be generated in parallel (launch the API calls together — several Bash calls in one message or background jobs), never one after another, with at most one regeneration pass per image. Save every file into artifacts/ and record its prompt/parameters in the task manifest.

entries.name: kb-retriever
entries.summary: Search and answer questions over a local knowledge-base folder: layered index navigation, then grep/read (PDF and spreadsheet handling included) instead of loading whole files.
entries.why: Lets a session answer from a folder of documents without reading everything into context.

entries.name: mmx-cli
entries.summary: MiniMax platform CLI (binary `mmx`): text/image-to-video generation and narration audio rendered to real media files.
entries.why: The video pack option for goals whose deliverable is an actual video file rather than a web presentation.

workflow.instruction: Generate video/audio with the mmx CLI. Save every rendered file into artifacts/ and record its prompt/parameters in the task manifest.

entries.name: ffmpeg
entries.summary: ffmpeg/ffprobe: verify video metadata (duration, resolution, codec) and extract frames so reviewers can look at them.
entries.why: Video goals get objective must checks (ffprobe) and frame extraction for review; without it acceptance falls back to file-exists checks.

entries.name: image-generation
entries.summary: Image generation via Gemini (default gemini-3-pro-image-preview) or OpenAI gpt-image; the model name routes the provider. Skill + MCP server + CLI in one plugin.
entries.why: An image pack option with real API generation out of the box; works with either a Gemini or an OpenAI key from Settings.

workflow.instruction: Generate with this skill (Gemini by default; a gpt-image/dall-e model name switches to OpenAI). Save every file into artifacts/ and record its prompt/parameters in the task manifest.

entries.name: imagegen-frontend-web
entries.summary: taste-skill's art-direction framework for generating web UI/product reference visuals: composition rules, section-by-section imagery, an opinionated design language. Requires an image-generation tool; instructions alone do not generate images.
entries.why: The taste image pack option: strong visual direction for UI-flavoured imagery instead of generic renders. Headless Foundry sessions do not inherit image tools from the Codex desktop app. Configure a permitted image tool separately or use prompt-only output; ChatGPT sign-in does not supply API credentials.

workflow.instruction: Follow its art direction when composing and generating web-oriented visuals. Save every file into artifacts/ and record its prompt/parameters in the task manifest. First verify that an image-generation tool is available; otherwise produce prompts and report generation unavailable without claiming images were created.

entries.name: imagegen-frontend-mobile
entries.summary: taste-skill's art-direction framework for generating mobile UI/product reference visuals: composition rules, section-by-section imagery, an opinionated design language. Requires an image-generation tool; instructions alone do not generate images.
entries.why: The taste image pack option: strong visual direction for UI-flavoured imagery instead of generic renders. Headless Foundry sessions do not inherit image tools from the Codex desktop app. Configure a permitted image tool separately or use prompt-only output; ChatGPT sign-in does not supply API credentials.

workflow.instruction: Follow its art direction when composing and generating mobile-oriented visuals. Save every file into artifacts/ and record its prompt/parameters in the task manifest. First verify that an image-generation tool is available; otherwise produce prompts and report generation unavailable without claiming images were created.

entries.name: design-taste-frontend
entries.summary: taste-skill's flagship (v2): design principles for AI-built frontends — stronger layout, typography, motion and spacing instead of generic output.
entries.why: A design pack option focused on taste rules rather than searchable databases; pairs with the taste imagegen image pack.

workflow.instruction: Invoke it before writing markup or styles and follow its layout/typography/motion/spacing principles; say which of its directions you applied.
Judge the UI against its principles: generic layouts, default spacing and lifeless typography are worth blockers when the skill was mandated.

entries.name: hyperframes
entries.summary: Core Hyperframes framework: HTML compositions, timeline, rendering concepts.
entries.why: The hyperframes video pack: motion-graphics editing/rendering (HTML+GSAP → real video) — the deliberate alternative to API text-to-video for demos, lessons and brand clips.

entries.name: make-a-video
entries.summary: End-to-end flow: from idea to a rendered video through the Hyperframes pipeline.
entries.why: The hyperframes video pack: motion-graphics editing/rendering (HTML+GSAP → real video) — the deliberate alternative to API text-to-video for demos, lessons and brand clips.

workflow.instruction: Build videos through the Hyperframes pipeline: follow the skill to scaffold the project in this workspace (npm install; needs Node 20+, FFmpeg, Chrome), author compositions, then render the final files into artifacts/ and record parameters in the task manifest.

entries.name: gsap
entries.summary: GSAP animation patterns for composition motion.
entries.why: The hyperframes video pack: motion-graphics editing/rendering (HTML+GSAP → real video) — the deliberate alternative to API text-to-video for demos, lessons and brand clips.

entries.name: short-form-video
entries.summary: Short-form (vertical/social) video conventions on the same pipeline.
entries.why: The hyperframes video pack: motion-graphics editing/rendering (HTML+GSAP → real video) — the deliberate alternative to API text-to-video for demos, lessons and brand clips. Requires a scaffolded Hyperframes student-kit project, including its root scripts/docs; copying this skill alone does not install those project dependencies.

entries.name: reverse-engineer-anything
entries.summary: REA's own workflow for the rea tools: open the target, trace the feature, keep the evidence, state the limits.
entries.why: With the rea MCP server installed, a worker studying a reference app or an undocumented interface follows a method instead of poking at tools; the investigation of a goal's reference uses it too.

workflow.instruction: When you must understand a shipped app, an SDK or an interface without documentation (the goal's reference included), invoke it and use the rea tools: keep the evidence behind each conclusion and build your own implementation from it — never copy proprietary code, never bypass a licence or a login.
Invoke it to analyse the goal's reference with the rea tools; the report states what the evidence shows, its limits, and what to build — never proprietary code copied out.

entries.name: cad
entries.summary: Creates and edits parametric CAD models (build123d) from plain-language or image requests; STEP as the main output, STL, 3MF and GLB on request; measures geometry and renders snapshots.
entries.why: The heart of a cad goal: the model contract (a Python source that builds and exports STEP when run), cadgen's geometry checks, and the snapshots the review reads. The plugin also ships the `cad` MCP server (the viewer), allowed for sessions once installed.

warmup.note: downloading the CAD runtime (Python 3.13 and OpenCASCADE, a few hundred MB, once)

workflow.instruction: Invoke it first and follow its model contract: a build123d source that builds and exports STEP when run, geometry measured with cadgen checks, and front, top, right and isometric snapshots of every deliverable written to artifacts/ for the review.
Use its inspection workflow to measure the delivered geometry against the Brief's dimensions; a deliverable without snapshots, or with dimensions off the Brief, is a blocker.

Use its inspection workflow to measure every deliverable of the goal against the Brief's dimensions and check that the manifest lists each file with its snapshots; a missing snapshot or a dimension off the Brief is a blocker.

entries.name: step-parts
entries.summary: Finds, evaluates and downloads off-the-shelf STEP parts (screws, bearings, motors, servos, connectors) from the step.parts catalog.
entries.why: An assembly with a named purchasable part gets the real part's geometry instead of a guessed placeholder, with its provenance recorded.

workflow.instruction: Before modelling a placeholder for a named off-the-shelf part (a motor, bearing, screw, connector), search step.parts and record the part id and provenance in the manifest.

entries.name: engineering-drawing
entries.summary: Dimensioned engineering drawings from a part, as a PDF: views, hidden lines, dimensions, hole callouts, title block.
entries.why: A part meant for a machine shop or a review needs a drawing, not only a model.

workflow.instruction: When the Brief asks for a drawing, produce the dimensioned PDF with it and list it in the manifest next to the model.

entries.name: dxf
entries.summary: 2D DXF drawings (profiles, templates, gaskets, cut layouts) from Python sources or CAD geometry.
entries.why: Laser cutting, routing and sheet metal take 2D profiles; this writes them from the same source as the model.

workflow.instruction: For 2D profiles, templates, gaskets and cut layouts, produce the DXF with it from the model's source, never by hand.

entries.name: urdf
entries.summary: Robot structure files: links, joints, limits, inertials and meshes.
entries.why: A robot's description belongs to the same goal as its parts; this keeps the file consistent with the geometry.

workflow.instruction: For a robot's structure file (links, joints, limits, inertials, meshes), write it with this skill from the modelled parts.

entries.name: srdf
entries.summary: MoveIt planning groups, end effectors, poses and collision rules on top of a URDF.
entries.why: Motion planning needs the semantic layer over the URDF; this writes it against the actual robot file.

workflow.instruction: For MoveIt planning groups, end effectors, poses and collision rules, write the SRDF with it against the goal's URDF.

entries.name: sdf
entries.summary: Simulator models and worlds: frames, physics, sensors and lights.
entries.why: A part or robot that is simulated needs an SDF that matches its geometry and mass properties.

workflow.instruction: For simulator models and worlds (frames, physics, sensors, lights), write the SDF with it from the modelled parts.

entries.name: dfam-check
entries.summary: Measures a mesh's printability per process: wall thickness, overhangs, support volume and build orientation.
entries.why: A part that prints badly is a defect the geometry alone does not show; the check gives measured evidence before the review.

workflow.instruction: For a part to be 3D-printed, run it before you finish (wall thickness, overhangs, support volume, orientation for the process the Brief names) and record the measurements in the manifest.
For printed parts, check the manifest's DfAM measurements against the process the Brief names, and run it yourself when they are missing.
For printed parts, check the manifest's DfAM measurements against the process the Brief names, and run it yourself when they are missing.

entries.name: dfm
entries.summary: Reviews a part for sheet metal, CNC machining or injection moulding with measured evidence (draft, undercuts, projected area) and the cited rule behind each finding.
entries.why: Manufacturability is part of correctness for a machined or moulded part; the findings cite the rule they rest on.

workflow.instruction: For CNC, sheet metal or injection moulding parts, review the part with it before you finish and record the cited findings in the manifest.
For CNC, sheet metal or injection moulding parts, read the manifest's DFM findings and run it yourself when they are missing; an unaddressed must-fix finding is a blocker.
For CNC, sheet metal or injection moulding parts, read the manifest's DFM findings and run it yourself when they are missing; an unaddressed must-fix finding is a blocker.

entries.name: gcode
entries.summary: Slices models into printer-ready G-code with OrcaSlicer and the person's own printer presets, headless.
entries.why: Printer-ready output is a deliverable some goals ask for; the slice runs on this computer with OrcaSlicer's command line.

workflow.instruction: When the Brief asks for printer-ready output, slice headless with OrcaSlicer's command line and the person's presets; never open the slicer's window.

entries.name: sendcutsend
entries.summary: Preflight reports for DXF and STEP uploads to SendCutSend: upload readiness, material and service checks against the current official sources.
entries.why: A cut-and-bend order fails at upload for reasons the model never shows; the report finds them first and never places an order.

workflow.instruction: Before a DXF or STEP is meant for a SendCutSend order, write its preflight report against the current official sources and attach it to the manifest.

entries.name: bambu-labs
entries.summary: Hands a sliced file to Bambu Connect, or an unsliced model to Bambu Studio, on this computer; the person picks the printer and starts the print there.
entries.why: It opens desktop apps on this computer, so unattended sessions do not see it until Settings → Safety → Desktop apps & printers is on.
